extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and law students studying patent infringement
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for determining when acts (making, using, selling, or procuring) constitute infringement of patents (machines, manufactures, compositions, and arts), with evidentiary and jurisdictional guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of 'using' a patented machine
rubrics_metrics.description: A using of a machine may be proved when the party charged has used it himself, has employed others to use it for him, or has profited by the use of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text states: "a using of a machine is to be taken as proved, either when the party charged has used it himself or has employed others to use it for him, or has profited by the use of it." The treatise explains that where one procures another to do work on a machine for his advantage he can be restrained; workmen aiding may be treated as principals to prevent evasions. Factual proof must overcome sworn denials (see evidentiary criterion below).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for acts done through agents or by ordering others (qui facit per alium)
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant may be held liable for infringement if he procures, orders, or causes others to make or use the patented invention, even if not personally performing the acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: giving an order to manufacture a patented article on a model furnished by a third person led to infringement even where defendants initially lacked knowledge of the patent. The maxim 'qui facit per alium, facit per se' is invoked; acting as agent of an infringer may subject one to damages and injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of a patented machine vs sale of materials
rubrics_metrics.description: To constitute infringement by 'sale' the act must be a sale of a complete machine for use as the patented machine, not merely a sale of the materials (separate or combined) that compose it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court held that "a sale of the materials of a patented machine... is not an infringement," e.g., a sheriff selling materials at execution (even complete materials) was not liable when he sold merely the materials without guaranteeing or selling the right to use the machine. Liability arises when the sale conveys the right (express or implied) to use the machine in the patented manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale/transfer of products made by patented machine generally not infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A sale of articles produced by a patented machine or by a patented process is generally not an infringement of the patent on the machine/process, unless the seller is connected with the use of the patented machine or process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise explains the policy: the patent protects the thing patented (machine/process), not the product; products when sold 'mingle with the common mass of property.' However, if the seller 'is connected with the use of the machine' (e.g., constructed or used it, or acted in concert with its user), he may be enjoined and be liable in damages; the extent of sales can help measure liability. An assignment of exclusive territorial rights does not generally prohibit the assignee from vending products outside the territory (Supreme Court rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts that infringe patents on manufactures or compositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patent is for a 'manufacture' or 'composition of matter,' infringement will occur by making, using, or selling the thing itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assuming 'manufacture' means the vendible, tangible product, such patents are infringed by making, using, or selling the subject matter. The statute vests the exclusive right to use the thing itself in the patentee; strictly speaking, any use (including consumption) could be an infringement, but public policy may limit enforcement against innocent consumers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability regarding perishable/consumable patented products
rubrics_metrics.description: For patented things that perish in use (e.g., medicines), those who sell or give them to others to be consumed may be regarded as using the invention and be held responsible for infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While consumers might technically be liable, courts recognize the impracticality and potential public inconvenience of penalizing purchasers unaware of infringement. Nonetheless the treatise states that in strictness the seller/giver who causes consumption may be held responsible because both seller and consumer 'make use of the invention to the injury of the patentee.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent requirement for illegal 'making'
rubrics_metrics.description: The making of a patented machine is an offense under the statute only when done with intent to use for profit (i.e., with intent to infringe), not when made for mere philosophical experiment or to test the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Whittemore v. Cutter: making must be 'with an intent to use for profit, and not for the mere purpose of philosophical experiment, or to ascertain the verity and exactness of the specification.' Thus innocent experimental making is not treated as an offense; intent to deprive the owner of lawful rewards is relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: When an art (process) is patented: infringement by practicing the art
rubrics_metrics.description: If an art (process) is the subject of a patent, infringement occurs by exercising or practicing the same art — putting the patented process into practice constitutes a 'using' of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ordering silk to be made by the same process and having it executed was held sufficient to satisfy allegations that defendant 'made, used, and put in practice the plaintiff's invention.' Conversely, executing an order for another may also constitute infringement (see related examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for infringement: substantial identity (same principle/modus operandi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement depends on whether the accused thing is the same in substance — a substantial identity — whether expressed as 'same principle,' 'same modus operandi,' or equivalent language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise emphasizes this is a fact-intensive enquiry: 'It is a copy of the thing described in the specification ... either without variation, or with only such variations as are consistent with its being in substance the same thing.' What constitutes substantial identity cannot be fully stated generally; courts look to individual cases and skilled testimony for illustrations. Judges have said similarity 'in principle' can indicate infringement, but 'principle' must be carefully defined (see next criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'principle' of an invention (how to identify essential features)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'principle' of an invention refers to the peculiar device, structure, constituent parts, or modus operandi essential to producing the result — not to elementary scientific principles common to many devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance includes: ascertain the result to be obtained; whatever is essential to that object, independent of mere form and proportions, may be considered the principle. Story: 'By the principles of a machine... is not meant the original elementary principles of motion ... but the modus operandi, the peculiar device or manner of producing any given effect.' Skilled witnesses can assist, but care is required because 'principle' may be understood differently by different minds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of substantial identity to machines
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine infringes if an accused machine incorporates the substance of the patentee's invention — i.e., by an arrangement of mechanism which performs the same service or produces the same effect in the same way or substantially the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'it will be infringed by a machine which incorporates in its structure and operation the substance of the invention; that is, by an arrangement of mechanism, which performs the same service, or produces the same effect in the same way, or substantially in the same way.' This is the concrete application of the substantial identity test for machines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard before issuing injunctions (affidavit vs sworn answer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts will not issue an injunction based solely on the affidavit of a single witness when opposed by a sworn, responsive answer; 'something more' than one witness's affidavit is required to overcome such an answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Isaac/Clement example the court refused to issue an injunction against Isaac on Pratt's affidavit alone, because Isaac had a sworn answer denying use; the court held that more evidence would be necessary to overcome the answer. The treatise cites cases showing that an affidavit of a single, non-explicit-witness is often insufficient to overcome a defendant's sworn denial.
